cse-2008-cs-67.approach: Count how many bits are needed to name what each entry points to: third-level entries point to 4 KB frames, while first- and second-level entries point to page tables whose size is fixed by the 9-bit indices.
cse-2008-cs-67.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Physical address | 36 bits |
| Frame | 4 KB = $2^{12}$ B |
| PTE | 4 B |
| Index bits L1 / L2 / L3 | 2 / 9 / 9 |

steps.title: Third-level entries point to frames
steps.body: Number of frames $=\dfrac{2^{36}}{2^{12}}=2^{24}$, so a third-level entry needs **24 bits** of frame number.

steps.title: Size of a second/third-level table
steps.body: Each such table is indexed by 9 bits: $2^{9}$ entries $\times 4$ B $=2^{11}$ B $=2$ KB.

steps.title: Bits to locate a 2 KB table
steps.body: Tables are 2 KB-aligned, so the low 11 bits of their base address are 0. The entry must hold $36-11=$ **25 bits**. This applies to first-level entries (pointing to second-level tables) and second-level entries (pointing to third-level tables).

steps.title: Result
steps.body: First, second, third level: **25, 25 and 24** bits — option (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: 20 bits would address only $2^{20}$ frames of 4 KB = 4 GB, but physical memory is $2^{36}$ B = 64 GB.
24 bits is right only for the last level; inner tables are 2 KB, not 4 KB, so they need 25 bits.
Uses 24 for inner levels (assumes 4 KB tables) and 20 for frames — both wrong.
25 bits locate a 2 KB-aligned table in 64 GB; 24 bits name a 4 KB frame.

pitfalls: Assuming every page table occupies a whole 4 KB frame — here the 9-bit-indexed tables are only 2 KB.
cse-2008-cs-67.verification: $2^{25}\times 2^{11}=2^{36}$ and $2^{24}\times2^{12}=2^{36}$, both covering the full physical space.

cse-2008-cs-68.approach: Since R and S share only the key attributes P and Q, the natural join pairs tuples with equal (P, Q); compare each query with $\Pi_P(\Pi_{P,Q}(R)\cap\Pi_{P,Q}(S))$.

steps.title: Query I
steps.body: $R\bowtie S$ joins on the common attributes $\{P,Q\}$, so it keeps exactly the $(P,Q)$ pairs present in both. $\Pi_P$ gives the P of those common pairs.

steps.title: Queries III and IV
steps.body: III is directly $\Pi_P(\Pi_{P,Q}(R)\cap\Pi_{P,Q}(S))$. IV uses $A-(A-B)=A\cap B$, so it is the same as III. Both equal I.

steps.title: Query II differs
steps.body: $\Pi_P(R)\bowtie\Pi_P(S)=\Pi_P(R)\cap\Pi_P(S)$ only matches P, ignoring Q. Counter-example: R has a tuple with $(P,Q)=(1,a)$ and S one with $(1,b)$: II gives $\{1\}$, while I, III and IV give $\varnothing$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: I, III and IV are equivalent — option (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: II is not equivalent to I (counter-example with same P, different Q).
Misses IV, which equals III because $A-(A-B)=A\cap B$.
Includes II, which matches on P alone.
I, III and IV all return P of the $(P,Q)$ pairs common to R and S.

pitfalls: Projecting to P before joining loses the Q constraint.
cse-2008-cs-68.verification: Checked with the two-tuple counter-example: II returns {1}, the others return the empty set.

cse-2008-cs-69.approach: Find all candidate keys of each scheme, then test BCNF/3NF/2NF against each FD that applies.

steps.title: Keys of Book

steps.title: Book is 2NF but not 3NF
steps.body: FD III: {Publisher, Title, Year} $\to$ Price. The LHS is not a superkey and Price is non-prime, so this is a transitive dependency — **not 3NF**. It is not partial: {Publisher, Title, Year} is not a proper subset of any key. No non-prime attribute depends on part of a key, so Book is **in 2NF**.

steps.title: Collection
steps.body: Collection(Title, Author, Catalog_no) has Title Author $\to$ Catalog_no and Catalog_no $\to$ Title Author. Both LHS are keys, so it is in **BCNF**, hence also in 3NF.

steps.title: Pick the statement
steps.body: Book: 2NF (not 3NF). Collection: 3NF (in fact BCNF). Option (C) is the only true statement.

answer.value: Book is in 2NF and Collection is in 3NF

Book is not in 3NF.

Collection is in BCNF, not '2NF only'.

cse-2008-cs-70.approach: A secondary index on a key field is dense: one entry (key + block pointer) per record. Divide by the index blocking factor level by level.

steps.title: Index blocking factor
steps.body: Entry size $=6+10=16$ B. Entries per block $=\lfloor 1024/16\rfloor=64$.

steps.title: First level (dense)
steps.body: 16384 records give 16384 entries: $16384/64=256$ blocks.

steps.title: Second level
steps.body: One entry per first-level block: $256/64=4$ blocks (a third level would have 1 block).

steps.title: Result
steps.body: 256 and 4 — option (C).

optionAnalysis.reason: Indexes data blocks (sparse) and miscounts; a secondary index must be dense.
128 would need 128 entries per block (8 B each); entries here are 16 B.
$16384/64=256$ first-level blocks, $256/64=4$ second-level blocks.
512 would need 32 entries per block; $1024/16$ is 64.

pitfalls: Using the data file's block count (sparse index) for a secondary index — the file is ordered on a different field, so every record needs an entry.
cse-2008-cs-70.verification: Data file has $1024/32=32$ records per block, i.e. 512 data blocks — irrelevant for a dense secondary index.

cse-2008-cs-71.approach: Split the 32-bit address into tag, set index and offset, then multiply the tag width by the number of cache lines.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Cache | 64 KB, 2-way, 16 B blocks |
| Address | 32-bit virtual |
| ARR | 1024×1024 doubles (8 B), row major, starts at page 0xFF000 |

steps.body: Offset 4 bits, index 11 bits, tag $=32-11-4=17$ bits.

cse-2008-cs-72.approach: Two addresses share a cache set when they differ by a multiple of (number of sets × block size) = $2^{11}\times16=32$ KB.
cse-2008-cs-72.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Cache | 64 KB, 2-way, 16 B blocks |
| Address | 32-bit virtual |
| ARR | 1024×1024 doubles (8 B), row major, starts at page 0xFF000 |

steps.title: Index period
steps.body: Index = address bits 4–14. Addresses map to the same set iff their difference is a multiple of $2^{15}$ B $=32$ KB.

steps.title: Row size
steps.body: One row $=1024\times8=8192$ B $=8$ KB, so ARR[i][0] is at offset $8i$ KB.

steps.title: Find the match
steps.body: ARR[4][0] is at $4\times8=32$ KB: same index as ARR[0][0]. ARR[5][0] is at 40 KB, ARR[0][4] at 32 B, ARR[0][5] at 40 B — all different sets.

optionAnalysis.reason: Offset 32 B is 2 blocks later: set index differs by 2.
Offset 32 KB $=2^{15}$ B, exactly one full index period.
Offset 40 B lies in block 2: different set.
Offset 40 KB is 8 KB past the period: set differs by 512.

pitfalls: Using the cache size (64 KB) as the period; for a 2-way cache the period is cache size / 2.
cse-2008-cs-72.verification: The base 0xFF000000 is 32 KB-aligned, so only the relative offsets decide the set.

cse-2008-cs-73.approach: The loop walks memory sequentially; each 16 B block holds two doubles, so every block gives one miss followed by one hit.
cse-2008-cs-73.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Cache | 64 KB, 2-way, 16 B blocks |
| Address | 32-bit virtual |
| ARR | 1024×1024 doubles (8 B), row major, starts at page 0xFF000 |

steps.title: Doubles per block
steps.body: $16/8=2$ doubles per block.

steps.title: Access pattern
steps.body: Row-major traversal touches ARR[i][j], ARR[i][j+1], … in address order. The first access to a block misses (cold, no prefetch), the second hits. Blocks are never revisited, so conflicts do not matter.

steps.title: Hit ratio
steps.body: $\dfrac{1\text{ hit}}{2\text{ accesses}}=50\%$.

optionAnalysis.reason: Would need one element per block, or eviction between a block's two uses.
Would need 4 elements per block with 3 misses, which does not happen here.
One miss and one hit per 16 B block.
Would need 4 doubles per block (32 B blocks).

pitfalls: Counting conflict misses — each block is used twice in a row and never again, so replacement is irrelevant.

cse-2008-cs-74.approach: f1 recomputes subproblems with two recursive calls (Fibonacci-like call tree, exponential); f2 is a single loop (linear).

steps.title: Function f1
steps.body: $T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2)+c$, the Fibonacci recurrence, so $T(n)=\Theta(\varphi^n)$ with $\varphi\approx1.618$ — exponential. Among the options this is written $\Theta(2^n)$ (it is $O(2^n)$).

steps.title: Function f2
steps.body: One loop from 2 to $n$ with $O(1)$ work per iteration: $\Theta(n)$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Exponential and linear — option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: f1 is not linear: no memoisation, two calls per level.
f1 exponential (two-branch recursion), f2 linear loop.
Swaps the two.
f2 does constant work per iteration.

cse-2008-cs-75.approach: Both compute $a_n=2a_{n-1}+3a_{n-2}$ with $a_0=0,a_1=1$: f2 keeps $Y[i]=2X[i]$, $Z[i]=3X[i]$, so $X[i]=2X[i-1]+3X[i-2]$. Tabulate up to $n=8$.

steps.body: Roots of $x^2=2x+3$ are $3$ and $-1$: $a_n=\dfrac{3^n-(-1)^n}{4}$. $a_8=\dfrac{6561-1}{4}=1640$. Both functions return **1640** — option (C).

59 is far too small (the sequence grows like $3^n/4$).
Both functions compute the same recurrence; $a_8=1640$.
f2 does not differ from f1.

cse-2008-cs-76.approach: By definition, the delay slot is the instruction placed right after the branch in memory; it always executes before control transfers.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: With delayed branching, the instruction in the slot (the next sequential instruction in memory after the branch) is always executed, whether or not the branch is taken; only then does the branch take effect.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Only the next sequential instruction in memory is guaranteed to run on both outcomes — option (A).

answer.value: The instruction following the branch in memory is executed

optionAnalysis.reason: This is exactly the delay-slot semantics.
The fall-through path continues after the slot, and only when the branch is not taken.
The target instruction runs only when taken, after the slot.
The point of delayed branching is to avoid lengthening the branch.

pitfalls: Confusing the delay slot with branch prediction (which speculates on one path).
cse-2008-cs-76.verification: Consistent with Q77: the slot must hold an instruction safe to run on both paths.

cse-2008-cs-77.approach: An instruction can move into the delay slot (after the branch) only if neither the instructions it jumps over nor the branch itself depend on it.

steps.title: Dependences
steps.body: I1 writes R2, read by I3. I2 writes R4, read by I4. I3 writes R1, read by I4 and by the branch (R1 == 0). I4 is a store: it writes memory, no register.

steps.title: Check each candidate
steps.body:
- I1 after the branch: I3 would read an old R2. ✗
- I2: I4 would use an old R4. ✗
- I3: the branch would test an old R1. ✗
- I4: reads R1 and R4 (already computed); nothing after it depends on it, and it executes on both paths anyway. ✓

steps.title: Result
steps.body: Only **I4** — option (D).

optionAnalysis.reason: I3 needs R2 from I1.
I4 needs R4 from I2.
The branch condition needs R1 from I3.
The store has no dependants and runs regardless of the outcome.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the branch itself reads R1 produced by I3.
cse-2008-cs-77.verification: The reordered sequence I1, I2, I3, BRANCH, I4 produces identical register and memory state on both paths.

cse-2008-cs-78.approach: Classify valid strings by their last bit: ending in 1 extends any valid string of length $n-1$; ending in 0 must end in '10', extending any valid string of length $n-2$.

cse-2008-cs-80.approach: For element $a_i$, either leave it out (a subset of the first $i-1$ sums to $j$) or include it once (a subset of the first $i-1$ sums to $j-a_i$); OR the two.

steps.title: Exclude $a_i$
steps.body: If $a_i$ is not used, the sum $j$ must come from $a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1}$: TRUE if $X[i-1,j]$.

steps.title: Include $a_i$ once
steps.body: The remaining $j-a_i$ must be formed from $a_1,\ldots,a_{i-1}$: $X[i-1,j-a_i]$. Using $X[i,\cdot]$ would allow reusing $a_i$.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Either choice suffices, so OR them: $X[i,j]=X[i-1,j]\vee X[i-1,j-a_i]$ — option (B).

cse-2008-cs-84.approach: Trace the loop on each case. The bug is $i=k$: once $j=i+1$, $k=i$ and if $Y[k]<x$ nothing changes, so the loop never terminates.

steps.title: Infinite loop
steps.body: From $i=8,j=9$: $k=\lfloor17/2\rfloor=8$, $Y[8]=2<x$ so $i=8$ again; $i<j$ stays true and $Y[k]\ne x$ — the loop never ends. The program **fails** on (C).

- (A) $x<10$ in 1..10: e.g. $x=9$: k = 4, 6, 7, 8 → found. Small $x$ moves $j$ down until $i=j=0$.
- (B) $x<1$: always $j=k$, so $j$ shrinks to 0 and the loop stops, printing 'not in the array' correctly.
- (D) every even $x$ in range is present and is found (e.g. $x=18$: k = 4, 6, 7, 8 → found).

cse-2008-cs-85.approach: Make every iteration shrink the interval $[i,j]$ by excluding the probed index $k$: $i=k+1$ on the right branch, $j=k-1$ on the left.

steps.title: Why the bug exists
steps.body: With $i=k$ the interval does not shrink when $j=i+1$ (since then $k=i$), giving the infinite loop of Q84.

steps.body: $i=k+1$ / $j=k-1$ removes $k$ every time, so $j-i$ strictly decreases and the loop terminates. Re-run Q84's case: k = 4 → i = 5, k = 7 → i = 8, k = 8 → i = 9; $i<j$ fails and it prints 'not in the array'. Correct.

steps.body: (B) moves the bounds the wrong way (the interval can grow). (C) still sets $i=k$ and hangs on the same input. (D) inverts the loop condition, so the search stops after one probe unless the target is hit immediately.
